entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret |H(j\omega)| as the frequency-dependent amplitude scaling applied by a continuous-time LTI system to sinusoidal inputs, using its variation over \omega to identify which components are attenuated, passed, or amplified.

sections.section_title: Scaling One Sinusoidal Input by |H(j\omega_0)|

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=8\cos(5t)$ and $|H(j5)|=0.25$, what is the output amplitude?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the input amplitude by the gain at the same frequency. Here $8 \cdot 0.25 = 2$, so the output amplitude is $2$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=5\cos(2t)$ and $|H(j2)|=1.6$, what is the output amplitude?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same rule: output amplitude equals input amplitude times $|H(j\omega_0)|$. Here $5 \cdot 1.6 = 8$, so the output amplitude is $8$.

sections.section_title: Classifying One Frequency as Attenuated, Passed, or Amplified

prompt_blocks.text: At $\omega_1$, a system has $|H(j\omega_1)|=1.3$. How is the component at that frequency classified?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compare the magnitude gain to 1. Since $1.3>1$, the component at $\omega_1$ is amplified.

prompt_blocks.text: At $\omega_2$, a system has $|H(j\omega_2)|=1$. How is the component at that frequency classified?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compare the magnitude gain to 1. Since $|H(j\omega_2)|=1$, the component at $\omega_2$ is passed with the same amplitude.

sections.section_title: Comparing Magnitude Response at Two Frequencies

prompt_blocks.text: A system has $|H(j\omega_1)|=0.5$ and $|H(j\omega_2)|=1.4$. Which frequency produces the larger output amplitude for the same input sinusoid?

choice_blocks.text: The smaller gain produces the larger output.
You cannot tell because the input is the same.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compare the gains directly. Since $1.4>0.5$, the sinusoid at $\omega_2$ is scaled more, so its output amplitude is larger.

prompt_blocks.text: A system has $|H(j\omega_1)|=0.9$ and $|H(j\omega_2)|=0.6$. Which frequency produces the larger output amplitude for the same input sinusoid?

choice_blocks.text: The smaller gain produces the larger output.
You cannot tell because the input is the same.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both gains are below 1, so both components are attenuated. Since $0.9>0.6$, the component at $\omega_1$ is less attenuated, so its output amplitude is larger.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Magnitude-Response Curve Across Frequency

image_slots.image_description: A clean instructional line plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with a bold horizontal reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Draw one continuous magnitude-response curve that sits above 1 over a low-frequency band, stays near 1 over a middle band, and falls below 1 over a high-frequency band. Label the horizontal axis with $\omega$ and the vertical axis with $|H(j\omega)|$. Optionally mark one representative frequency in each band so the viewer can read the above, equal, and below-1 regions directly.

A clean instructional line plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with a bold horizontal reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Draw one continuous magnitude-response curve that sits below 1 over a low-frequency band, rises above 1 over a middle band, and falls below 1 again over a high-frequency band. Label the horizontal axis with $\omega$ and the vertical axis with $|H(j\omega)|$. Optionally mark one representative frequency in each band so the viewer can read the below, above, and below-1 regions directly.

prompt_blocks.text: Using the magnitude-response plot, which statement correctly describes the low-, middle-, and high-frequency regions relative to the unity line $|H(j\omega)|=1$?

choice_blocks.text: Low frequencies are amplified, middle frequencies are passed, and high frequencies are attenuated.
Low frequencies are attenuated, middle frequencies are amplified, and high frequencies are attenuated.
Low frequencies are amplified, middle frequencies are attenuated, and high frequencies are passed.
The plot shows phase behavior, not amplitude behavior.
Because the curve touches $|H(j\omega)|=1$, the system is all-pass.

questions.correct_answer: Low frequencies are amplified, middle frequencies are passed, and high frequencies are attenuated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read each band against $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Values above 1 amplify the sinusoid, values near 1 pass it unchanged, and values below 1 attenuate it.

prompt_blocks.text: Using the magnitude-response plot, which statement correctly describes the low-, middle-, and high-frequency regions relative to the unity line $|H(j\omega)|=1$?

choice_blocks.text: Low frequencies are amplified, middle frequencies are passed, and high frequencies are attenuated.
Low frequencies are attenuated, middle frequencies are amplified, and high frequencies are attenuated.
Low frequencies are attenuated, middle frequencies are passed, and high frequencies are amplified.
The curve’s rise and fall tell you the amplitude changes, not its height relative to 1.
Because the curve crosses $|H(j\omega)|=1$ twice, the system is all-pass.

questions.correct_answer: Low frequencies are attenuated, middle frequencies are amplified, and high frequencies are attenuated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same rule applies everywhere on the curve: compare each frequency band to $|H(j\omega)|=1$. Here the low and high bands are below 1, so they are attenuated, while the middle band is above 1, so it is amplified.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret \angle H(j\omega) as the frequency-dependent phase shift applied to each sinusoidal input component when using frequency response to characterize LTI filter behavior.

sections.section_title: Reading \angle H(j\omega) at a Single Frequency

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j6)=4e^{-j\pi/6}$, what phase shift applies to a sinusoidal input at $\omega=6$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the single frequency $\omega=6$, and the response is already in exponential form. For phase response, read the angle, not the magnitude, because the angle is the phase shift at that frequency.
So the phase shift at $\omega=6$ is $-\pi/6$, which is a phase lag of $\pi/6$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j2)=5\angle \pi/3$, which statement correctly describes the phase shift at $\omega=2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the single frequency $\omega=2$, and the response is written in polar form. For phase response, read the angle, not the magnitude.
Because the angle is positive, the system advances the sinusoid by $\pi/3$. So the correct description is phase lead of $\pi/3$.

sections.section_title: Applying Phase Response to a Sinusoidal Component

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=\cos(5t+\pi/6)$ and $\angle H(j5)=-\pi/4$, what is the output phase of the sinusoid?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same frequency and add the input phase to the system phase: $\pi/6+(-\pi/4)=-\pi/12$. The output phase is $-\pi/12$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=\cos(3t-\pi/8)$, $\angle H(j3)=\pi/3$, and $\angle H(j7)=-\pi/6$, what is the output phase of the sinusoid at $\omega=3$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\angle H(j3)$, not $\angle H(j7)$. Add the phases at $\omega=3$: $-\pi/8+\pi/3=5\pi/24$. So the output phase is $5\pi/24$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Positive and Negative Phase Shifts

prompt_blocks.text: If $\angle H(j3)=-\pi/2$, does the output at $\omega=3$ lead or lag the input, and by how much?

choice_blocks.text: It changes the output amplitude by $\pi/2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A negative phase value means lag or delay. Since $\angle H(j3)=-\pi/2<0$, the output at $\omega=3$ lags the input by $\pi/2$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $\angle H(j7)=\pi/4$, does the output at $\omega=7$ lead or lag the input, and by how much?

choice_blocks.text: It changes the output amplitude by $\pi/4$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A positive phase value means lead or advance. Since $\angle H(j7)=\pi/4>0$, the output at $\omega=7$ leads the input by $\pi/4$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Phase Shifts Across Frequencies

prompt_blocks.text: If $\angle H(j2)=\pi/2$ and $\angle H(j7)=-\pi/6$, which frequency component is more delayed?

choice_blocks.text: The $\omega=7$ component is more delayed, and the $\omega=2$ component is more advanced.
The $\omega=2$ component is more delayed because it has the larger phase magnitude.
The $\omega=7$ component is more advanced, and the $\omega=2$ component is more delayed.
The $\omega=2$ component is more delayed because positive phase means lag.
The comparison depends on the magnitude response, not the phase response.

questions.correct_answer: The $\omega=7$ component is more delayed, and the $\omega=2$ component is more advanced.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Positive phase means advance and negative phase means delay. Since $\angle H(j2)=\pi/2$ is positive and $\angle H(j7)=-\pi/6$ is negative, the $\omega=7$ component is more delayed.

prompt_blocks.text: If $\angle H(j4)=\pi/6$ and $\angle H(j6)=\pi/2$, which frequency component is more advanced?

choice_blocks.text: The $\omega=6$ component is more advanced, and the $\omega=4$ component is less advanced.
The $\omega=4$ component is more advanced because it has the smaller phase magnitude.
The $\omega=6$ component is more delayed, and the $\omega=4$ component is more advanced.
The $\omega=4$ component is more delayed because positive phase means lag.
The comparison depends on the magnitude response, not the phase response.

questions.correct_answer: The $\omega=6$ component is more advanced, and the $\omega=4$ component is less advanced.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both phases are positive, so both components are advanced. The larger positive phase at $\omega=6$ means a larger advance than at $\omega=4$, so $\omega=6$ is more advanced.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate low-frequency behavior by examining H(j\omega) as \omega approaches 0 and interpreting its magnitude and phase to decide how an LTI system scales, shifts, passes, or attenuates slowly varying inputs.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Low-Frequency Limit of H(j\omega)

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(j\omega)=\frac{1+j\omega}{2+j\omega}$, evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to 0}H(j\omega)$ and state the low-frequency gain and phase.

choice_blocks.text: $H(j0)=\frac12$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac12$ and the phase is $0$.
At $\omega=1$, $H(j1)=\frac{3+j}{5}$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac12$ and the phase is $0$.
$H(j0)=2$, so the low-frequency gain is $2$ and the phase is $0$.
$H(j0)=\frac{1+j\omega}{2+j\omega}$, so the limit still depends on $\omega$.

questions.correct_answer: $H(j0)=\frac12$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac12$ and the phase is $0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the low-frequency limit, so set $\omega=0$ and read the DC value.
Because the limit is a positive real number, the low-frequency gain is $\frac12$ and the phase is $0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(j\omega)=\frac{-3+j\omega}{2+j\omega}$, evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to 0}H(j\omega)$ and state the low-frequency gain and phase.

choice_blocks.text: $H(j0)=-\frac32$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac32$ and the phase is $\pi$.
$H(j0)=-\frac23$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac23$ and the phase is $\pi$.
$H(j0)=\frac{-3+j\omega}{2+j\omega}$, so the limit still depends on $\omega$.
At $\omega=1$, $H(j1)=\frac{-3+j}{2+j}$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac32$ and the phase is $\pi$.

questions.correct_answer: $H(j0)=-\frac32$, so the low-frequency gain is $\frac32$ and the phase is $\pi$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, the cue is the low-frequency limit, so substitute $\omega=0$.
A negative real limit has magnitude $\frac32$ and phase $\pi$, so the low-frequency component is inverted and scaled by $\frac32$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Low-Frequency Magnitude Scaling

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $H(j0)=\frac{3}{4}$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: It is attenuated by a factor of $\frac{3}{4}$.
It is amplified by a factor of $\frac{3}{4}$.
It is passed unchanged because only the phase matters at low frequency.
It is attenuated by a factor of $\frac{4}{3}$.
It is amplified by a factor of $\frac{4}{3}$.

questions.correct_answer: It is attenuated by a factor of $\frac{3}{4}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the low-frequency gain $|H(j0)|$. Since $\frac{3}{4}<1$, the system attenuates the slowly varying sinusoidal component, so the output amplitude is multiplied by $\frac{3}{4}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $H(j0)=2$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: It is amplified by a factor of $2$.
It is attenuated by a factor of $2$.
It is passed unchanged because any positive gain means no scaling.
It is amplified by a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$.
It is attenuated by a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.correct_answer: It is amplified by a factor of $2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is again the low-frequency gain $|H(j0)|$. Since $2>1$, the system amplifies the slowly varying sinusoidal component, so the output amplitude is multiplied by $2$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Low-Frequency Phase Shift

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $H(j0)=-3$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, which low-frequency phase shift and output description are correct?

choice_blocks.text: Phase shift $0$; the output is scaled by 3.
Phase shift $\pi$; the output is inverted and scaled by 3.
Phase shift $\pi/2$; the output is delayed and scaled by 3.
Phase shift $\pi$; the output is scaled by 3.
Phase shift $0$; the output is inverted and scaled by 3.

questions.correct_answer: Phase shift $\pi$; the output is inverted and scaled by 3.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A negative real low-frequency gain has angle $\pi$. Since $H(j0)=-3$, the magnitude is 3 and the slow sinusoid is flipped.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $H(j0)=-\frac{5}{4}$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, which low-frequency phase shift and output description are correct?

choice_blocks.text: Phase shift $0$; the output is scaled by $\frac{5}{4}$.
Phase shift $\pi$; the output is inverted and scaled by $\frac{5}{4}$.
Phase shift $\pi/2$; the output is delayed and scaled by $\frac{5}{4}$.
Phase shift $\pi$; the output is scaled by $\frac{5}{4}$.
Phase shift $0$; the output is inverted and scaled by $\frac{5}{4}$.

questions.correct_answer: Phase shift $\pi$; the output is inverted and scaled by $\frac{5}{4}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The sign of $H(j0)$ controls the phase classification. Because $H(j0)$ is negative and real, the phase shift is $\pi$; the magnitude $\frac{5}{4}$ scales the slow sinusoid.

sections.section_title: Deciding How Slowly Varying Inputs Change Through the System

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j0)=-2$ and $x(t)=A\cos(0.03t+\phi)$, what is the approximate output for this slowly varying component?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A negative low-frequency gain has magnitude $2$ and phase $\pi$, so the slow sinusoid is doubled and inverted while the frequency stays slow.

prompt_blocks.text: If $H(j0)=\frac{1}{3}e^{j\pi/2}$ and $x(t)=4A\cos(0.02t-\pi/6)$, what is the approximate output for this slowly varying component?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The gain has magnitude $\frac{1}{3}$ and phase $\pi/2$, so the amplitude is multiplied by $\frac{1}{3}$ and the phase is shifted by $\pi/2$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate high-frequency limits of |H(j\omega)| and \angle H(j\omega) to predict how an LTI system passes, attenuates, or phase-shifts rapidly varying sinusoidal components.

sections.section_title: Evaluating High-Frequency Magnitude Limits

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{-5j\omega+1}{4j\omega+7}$?

questions.correct_answer: $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|=\frac{5}{4}$, so very high-frequency components are amplified.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep only the leading $j\omega$ terms. Lower-order terms do not change the high-frequency magnitude.
Taking the magnitude removes the sign, so the limit is $\left|\frac{-5}{4}\right|=\frac{5}{4}$. Because this is greater than $1$, the system amplifies very high-frequency components.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{-2j\omega-9}{7j\omega+3}$?

questions.correct_answer: $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|=\frac{2}{7}$, so very high-frequency components are attenuated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, keep only the leading $j\omega$ terms. The lower-order constants disappear in the high-frequency limit.
The magnitude is $\left|\frac{-2}{7}\right|=\frac{2}{7}$. Since this is less than $1$, the system attenuates very high-frequency components.

sections.section_title: Evaluating High-Frequency Phase Limits

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\angle H(j\omega)$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{2-j\omega}{1+j\omega}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is a high-frequency phase question, so keep the leading terms and compare their angles, not their magnitudes.
The numerator contributes $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and the denominator contributes $\frac{\pi}{2}$, so the phase limit is $-\pi$. The magnitude limit would be $1$, but that is not the quantity being asked.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\angle H(j\omega)$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{3+j\omega}{2+j\omega}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Here both leading terms are positive imaginary terms, so their asymptotic angles match.
That gives $\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{2}=0$, so there is no asymptotic phase shift. The rapid sinusoid keeps its phase at high frequency.

sections.section_title: Using Dominant Powers of j\omega in High-Frequency Limits

prompt_blocks.text: What is the high-frequency magnitude limit of $H(j\omega)=\frac{5(j\omega)^2-3j\omega+1}{2(j\omega)^3+4(j\omega)^2-7}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator has one higher power of $j\omega$ than the numerator, so the dominant-power ratio leaves one factor of $1/(j\omega)$ after cancellation. That factor goes to $0$ in magnitude as $\omega\to\infty$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the high-frequency magnitude limit of $H(j\omega)=\frac{6(j\omega)^3-2j\omega+1}{4(j\omega)^3+5(j\omega)^2-7}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The numerator and denominator have the same highest power of $j\omega$, so the lower-order terms drop out. The high-frequency magnitude is the ratio of the leading coefficients, $\left|\frac{6}{4}\right|=\frac{3}{2}$.

sections.section_title: Predicting Rapid-Sinusoid Output from High-Frequency Gain and Phase

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=4\cos(\omega_0 t+\pi/8)$ and $H(j\omega)\to -\tfrac{1}{2}$ as $\omega\to\infty$, what is the approximate output for very large $\omega_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The limit $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ has magnitude $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and phase $\pi$. So the amplitude becomes $4\cdot \tfrac{1}{2}=2$, and the phase becomes $\pi/8+\pi=9\pi/8\equiv -7\pi/8$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=5\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$ and $H(j\omega)\to 2j$ as $\omega\to\infty$, what is the approximate output for very large $\omega_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The limit $2j$ has magnitude $2$ and phase $\pi/2$. So the amplitude becomes $5\cdot 2=10$, and the phase becomes $-\pi/4+\pi/2=\pi/4$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify low-pass behavior in H(j\omega) by comparing its magnitude at low and high frequencies and interpreting strong low-frequency passage with high-frequency attenuation as the system preserving slow sinusoidal components while suppressing rapid ones.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Strong Low-Frequency Passage from |H(j\omega)|

prompt_blocks.text: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 0.97$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.11$. Which statement best describes how it treats slow versus fast sinusoidal components?

choice_blocks.text: It is low-pass: slow components pass much more strongly than fast ones.
It is high-pass: fast components pass much more strongly than slow ones.
It is all-pass: both components are preserved equally.
It is phase-only: the magnitudes do not affect amplitude.
The comparison is inconclusive because both magnitudes are nonzero.

questions.correct_answer: It is low-pass: slow components pass much more strongly than fast ones.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low-frequency gain is close to $1$ while the high-frequency gain is much smaller. That means the slow sinusoidal component is passed with little attenuation and the fast one is strongly reduced, which is low-pass behavior.

prompt_blocks.text: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 1.05$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.18$. What is the best conclusion about its frequency-response behavior?

choice_blocks.text: It is high-pass because fast components pass much more strongly than slow ones.
It is all-pass because both magnitudes are nonzero.
It is phase-only because only phase matters here.
It is low-pass because slow components are preserved more strongly and fast ones are attenuated.
The comparison is inconclusive because the low-frequency gain is slightly above $1$.

questions.correct_answer: It is low-pass because slow components are preserved more strongly and fast ones are attenuated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Even though the low-frequency gain is slightly above $1$, it is still much larger than the high-frequency gain. That means the slow component is preserved much more strongly than the fast one, so the system is low-pass.

sections.section_title: Recognizing High-Frequency Attenuation from |H(j\omega)|

prompt_blocks.text: At $\omega = 60$, the magnitude response is $|H(j60)| = 0.04$. What happens to a sinusoidal input at that frequency?

choice_blocks.text: The output keeps frequency $60$ but its amplitude becomes $0.04$ of the input amplitude.
The output keeps frequency $60$ and its amplitude stays unchanged because the gain is nonzero.
The output is amplified at high frequency, so this is high-pass behavior.
The output keeps the same amplitude and only its phase changes.
All frequency components of the signal are reduced by a factor of $0.04$.

questions.correct_answer: The output keeps frequency $60$ but its amplitude becomes $0.04$ of the input amplitude.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A small value of $|H(j60)|$ means the system scales the sinusoid at $\omega = 60$ by a small factor.
The frequency stays $60$, but the amplitude shrinks. That is high-frequency attenuation, which is the high-frequency side of low-pass behavior.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal contains a rapid sinusoidal component at $\omega = 120$. If $|H(j120)| = 0.02$, which interpretation is most accurate?

choice_blocks.text: That rapid component is strongly attenuated at the same frequency, which supports low-pass behavior.
That rapid component is passed unchanged because it is still present in the output.
The system only changes the phase of that rapid component.
The low-frequency part is reduced by $0.02$ while the rapid part is preserved.
The system is high-pass because small high-frequency gain means high-frequency emphasis.

questions.correct_answer: That rapid component is strongly attenuated at the same frequency, which supports low-pass behavior.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read $|H(j120)| = 0.02$ as the gain applied to the rapid component at $\omega = 120$. The gain is tiny, so that component is heavily reduced rather than passed or changed only in phase.
The component keeps the same frequency but loses most of its amplitude. That is exactly the high-frequency attenuation pattern used to identify low-pass behavior.

sections.section_title: Comparing Low- and High-Frequency Magnitudes

prompt_blocks.text: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 0.9$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.4$. Which frequency is passed more strongly, and what filter behavior does that imply?

choice_blocks.text: The high-frequency component is passed more strongly, so the system is high-pass.
The system is all-pass because both magnitudes are nonzero.
The low-frequency component is passed more strongly, so the system is low-pass.
The numbers describe phase rather than magnitude, so the comparison is not useful.
No conclusion can be made from the comparison.

questions.correct_answer: The low-frequency component is passed more strongly, so the system is low-pass.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compare the two magnitudes directly. The low-frequency gain is larger, so the slow component is passed more strongly than the fast one.
Since $0.9 > 0.4$, the system preserves low-frequency content more strongly, which is the low-pass pattern.

prompt_blocks.text: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 1.4$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 1.1$. Which frequency is passed more strongly, and what filter behavior does that imply?

choice_blocks.text: The system is all-pass because both magnitudes exceed 1.
The low-frequency component is passed more strongly, so the system is low-pass.
The high-frequency component is passed more strongly, so the system is high-pass.
The values are phase values rather than magnitudes, so the comparison is not useful.
No conclusion can be made from the comparison.

questions.correct_answer: The low-frequency component is passed more strongly, so the system is low-pass.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The decision still comes from comparing the two magnitudes, not from checking whether either one is above 1. The low-frequency value is larger, so low frequencies are passed more strongly.
Since $1.4 > 1.1$, the system still shows low-pass behavior because the low-frequency component is favored over the high-frequency one.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Low-Pass Behavior for Sinusoidal Components

prompt_blocks.text: A low-pass system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{slow}})| \approx 1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{fast}})| \approx 0.05$ for $x(t)=\cos(\omega_{\text{slow}} t)+\cos(\omega_{\text{fast}} t)$. Which description best matches the output component by component?

choice_blocks.text: The slow cosine stays prominent, while the fast cosine is strongly attenuated.
The fast cosine stays prominent, while the slow cosine is strongly attenuated.
Both cosines are scaled by the same amount.
The system changes only phase, not amplitude.

questions.correct_answer: The slow cosine stays prominent, while the fast cosine is strongly attenuated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A low-pass system passes the small-$\omega$ term much more strongly than the large-$\omega$ term, so the slow sinusoid remains large and the fast sinusoid is suppressed.

prompt_blocks.text: A low-pass system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{slow}})| \approx 1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{fast}})| \approx 0.1$. If $x(t)=2\cos(\omega_{\text{fast}} t)+3\cos(\omega_{\text{slow}} t)$, which output approximation is best?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply each sinusoid by the gain at its own frequency. The slow term keeps nearly full amplitude, while the fast term is reduced by a factor of about $0.1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify high-pass behavior for an LTI filter from its magnitude response by comparing |H(j\omega)| at low and high frequencies and identifying low-frequency attenuation with high-frequency passage.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Low-Frequency Attenuation

prompt_blocks.text: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.12$ for small $\omega$ and $|H(j\omega)| \approx 1$ for large $\omega$. What does the small-$\omega$ magnitude say about the low-frequency components?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A gain around $0.12$ near $\omega=0$ is well below $1$, so the low-frequency components are attenuated rather than passed or amplified.

prompt_blocks.text: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.08$ near $\omega=0$ and stays close to $1$ at higher $\omega$. Which label best describes the low-frequency end of the response?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A gain near $0.08$ at $\omega=0$ is still well below $1$, so the low-frequency end of the response is attenuated.

sections.section_title: Recognizing High-Frequency Passage

prompt_blocks.text: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.97$ for large $\omega$. What does that say about high-frequency components?

choice_blocks.text: High-frequency components pass through with almost the same amplitude.
High-frequency components are amplified because the gain is close to $1$.
The filter must be low-pass because the low-frequency gain is small.
The large-$\omega$ value only tells you the phase shift.

questions.correct_answer: High-frequency components pass through with almost the same amplitude.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A magnitude of $0.97$ is close to $1$, so the high-frequency components are passed with little attenuation. It is not amplification because the gain is still below $1$.

prompt_blocks.text: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.11$ for small $\omega$ and $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.93$ for large $\omega$. What does the large-$\omega$ magnitude say about the high-frequency components?

choice_blocks.text: High-frequency components pass through with little attenuation.
The filter is low-pass because the low-frequency gain is small.
The large-$\omega$ value only tells you the phase shift.

questions.correct_answer: High-frequency components pass through with little attenuation.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The large-$\omega$ magnitude is close to $1$, so the high-frequency components pass through with nearly the same amplitude. The small low-frequency value just shows the low end is attenuated.

sections.section_title: Comparing Low- and High-Frequency Gain

prompt_blocks.text: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.25$ near $\omega=0$ and $|H(j\omega)| \approx 1.05$ for large $\omega$. Which gain is larger, and what does that comparison imply about the response?

choice_blocks.text: The high-frequency gain is larger, so the response rises with frequency and behaves like a high-pass filter.
The low-frequency gain is larger, so the response falls with frequency and behaves like a low-pass filter.
The gains are equal, so the response is all-pass.
The high-frequency gain is larger, so the response is band-pass.
The comparison is about phase, not magnitude.

questions.correct_answer: The high-frequency gain is larger, so the response rises with frequency and behaves like a high-pass filter.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the low-frequency and high-frequency values as $0.25$ and $1.05$, then compare them directly.
Because $1.05 > 0.25$, the high-frequency gain is larger. The low-frequency side is smaller, so low frequencies are attenuated more than high frequencies.
That means the magnitude response rises with frequency, so the filter behaves like a high-pass filter.

prompt_blocks.text: A filter has $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.60$ near $\omega=0$ and $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0.90$ for large $\omega$. What does that comparison tell you about the filter?

choice_blocks.text: The high-frequency gain is larger, so low frequencies are attenuated more than high frequencies and the filter behaves like a high-pass filter.
The low-frequency gain is larger, so high frequencies are attenuated more and the filter behaves like a low-pass filter.
The gains are equal, so the filter is all-pass.
The high-frequency gain is larger, so the filter is band-pass.
Because both gains are below $1$, the comparison cannot classify the filter.

questions.correct_answer: The high-frequency gain is larger, so low frequencies are attenuated more than high frequencies and the filter behaves like a high-pass filter.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The key comparison is $0.90 > 0.60$, so the high-frequency side has the larger gain.
Even though $0.90$ is still below $1$, it is larger than $0.60$, so high frequencies pass more strongly than low frequencies.
That comparison supports a high-pass classification because the magnitude response rises from low to high frequency.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Magnitude Response as High-Pass

prompt_blocks.text: Use the described magnitude response to classify the filter: $|H(j\omega)|$ is well below $1$ near $\omega=0$, then rises and approaches $1$ for large $\omega$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The plot is well below 1 near $\omega=0$ and rises to about 1 at large $\omega$. That means low frequencies are attenuated while high frequencies pass.
That is the high-pass pattern, not low-pass, band-pass, or all-pass.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the filter: $|H(j\omega)|$ is clearly smaller near $\omega=0$ than at high frequency, where the response levels off close to $1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low-frequency side is still much smaller than the high-frequency side. Low frequencies are attenuated, and the high-frequency end stays near unity, so the response passes high frequencies.
That rising low-to-high pattern is high-pass.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify a filter's passband behavior from its magnitude response by comparing low- and high-frequency gain to decide whether the LTI system is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

prompt_blocks.text: On the displayed magnitude-response curve, which statement correctly describes the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end relative to $|H(j\omega)|=1$?

choice_blocks.text: The low-frequency gain is above $1$ and the high-frequency gain is below $1$.
The low-frequency gain is below $1$ and the high-frequency gain is above $1$.
The low-frequency gain is above $1$ and the high-frequency gain is above $1$.
The low-frequency gain is below $1$ and the high-frequency gain is below $1$.
The curve rises from left to right, so the high-frequency gain is larger.

questions.correct_answer: The low-frequency gain is above $1$ and the high-frequency gain is below $1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the left side of the curve as the low-frequency gain and the right side as the high-frequency gain. Compare each end to the unity line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$.
So the low-frequency end is larger than the high-frequency end.

prompt_blocks.text: From the displayed magnitude-response curve, which comparison of the two ends is correct relative to the unity line?

choice_blocks.text: The low-frequency gain is above $1$ and the high-frequency gain is below $1$.
The low-frequency gain is below $1$ and the high-frequency gain is below $1$.
The low-frequency gain is below $1$ and the high-frequency gain is above $1$.
The low-frequency gain is above $1$ and the high-frequency gain is above $1$.
The curve falls from left to right, so the high-frequency gain is smaller.

questions.correct_answer: The low-frequency gain is below $1$ and the high-frequency gain is above $1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The step is only asking for the heights at the two ends of the curve. The left end is the low-frequency gain, and the right end is the high-frequency gain.
That gives the low-frequency end below the unity line and the high-frequency end above it.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low-frequency end is higher than the high-frequency end, so the filter passes low frequencies better than high frequencies. That makes it low-pass.

prompt_blocks.text: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, which filter class best fits?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low-frequency end is still higher than the high-frequency end, even though both ends are below unity. That end comparison still makes the filter low-pass.

prompt_blocks.text: The displayed magnitude-response curve has a lower low-frequency gain than high-frequency gain. Which filter class best fits?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The high-frequency end is higher than the low-frequency end, so the filter passes high frequencies better than low frequencies. That makes it high-pass.

prompt_blocks.text: This magnitude-response curve has a smaller gain at low frequency than at high frequency. Which filter class best fits?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The only cue that matters here is the ordering of the two ends. Since the high-frequency end is larger than the low-frequency end, the filter is high-pass.

prompt_blocks.text: The displayed magnitude-response curve has low- and high-frequency ends at about the same gain, while the middle region rises differently. Which classification fits?
Use the two ends of the curve, not the middle hump, to decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low- and high-frequency ends are about the same height, so the curve does not show a one-sided passband pattern.
Since neither end is larger, the filter is neither low-pass nor high-pass.

prompt_blocks.text: The displayed magnitude-response curve has low- and high-frequency ends at about the same gain, while the middle region dips differently. Which classification fits?
Use the two ends of the curve, not the middle notch, to decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low- and high-frequency ends sit at about the same gain, so the curve does not favor one side over the other.
That end comparison rules out both low-pass and high-pass, so the correct classification is neither.
